title: Pusaka docs
text: A Bitcoin Cash wallet with an inheritance plan built in. Learn to set up a plan and verify its transactions.

title: Wallet guide
text: Set up a wallet, manage your funds, and follow a family claim. Live app: https://astrorehan.github.io/pusaka-bch/ (mainnet) and https://astrorehan.github.io/pusaka-bch/chipnet/ (Chipnet, the test network). The demo at /wallet/demo opens a live example plan whose owner has gone quiet. Any visitor can open its claim or pay its heirs, with no wallet of their own: the plan pays the network fee. Create your own wallet to try the owner's actions.

title: Owner
text: Owner Open Wallet, choose Set up wallet, and connect Paytaca. Add heirs and choose equal shares, integer custom shares or the existing faraid family calculator. Verify addresses and the calculation before approving. Add three distinct trusted contacts. Choose inactivity and review periods. Enter an initial usable BCH balance. This creates a new Pusaka receive address. Keep at least 600 sats at the first ordinary wallet receive address for authorization. If necessary, use Prepare wallet, review that separate transaction, then review wallet creation. Approve each in Paytaca. Save the resulting plan JSON/link. Use Send for partial BCH payments. Protected change remains in Pusaka and the same transaction renews activity. I'm still here is the fallback. Receive shows the permanent BCH inbox. Incoming funds are protected without owner approval. Collect makes batched receipts spendable and charges the reviewed network fee. Incoming receipts never renew activity. During review, Stop claim or an ordinary BCH payment cancels the claim. An owner token send and Swap currently ask you to stop a pending claim first. Take funds back retires the current BCH balance. The old receive address still protects later receipts. Token holdings stay under the plan's family rules.

title: Family
text: Family Open the shared plan link or import its JSON. A contact connects their own wallet and chooses Confirm a claim. The first approval has no spending authority. The second distinct contact opens the full review period. Alternatively, anyone can open an inactivity claim after the network deadline. Wait for the anchor to confirm and its chain age to mature. The network clock can lag behind a phone. Pay the heirs submits the fixed BCH distribution. Afterward, Pay late receipts handles new BCH. Under Protected tokens, Pay heirs distributes one fungible receipt per transaction; the submitter provides BCH for token carriers and fees. All indivisible units go to the final heir.

title: Swap
text: Swap On Chipnet, open Swap for BCH / PSK. PSK is a test token, not an investment. Get a quote, inspect minimum return and fees, then review the complete transaction. The token output goes directly into your Pusaka token vault. Use that token address only for supported fungible tokens. The BCH inbox is a different address.

title: After reconnecting
text: After reconnecting Open the saved plan link or choose Open a plan and paste JSON. Public rules rebuild the same addresses, and the app discovers current state from the chain. Reconnect the correct wallet for owner or contact actions. Save an updated link after policy edits; old policy data fails closed instead of redirecting payouts. An accepted transaction still needs block confirmation. If submission times out, check its transaction ID and refresh before trying again. The local activity list records submissions from that browser, not a complete recovered chain history.

title: Demo narration
text: Demo narration Show the usable BCH balance, a partial payment renewing activity and a new receipt. Show two contacts opening review and the owner stopping a false claim. Then show a valid mature claim and the fixed multi-heir payout. Finish with the Cauldron swap and the token payout receipts in the verification record. The 512-second Chipnet review is a test configuration. New UI plans default to 90 days of inactivity and at least 7 days of review. Explain the initial move to a new address. Do not promise inheritance for untouched Paytaca or exchange funds. The real phone/mainnet checks still pending are listed in the release evidence.

title: Pusaka in one minute
text: Pusaka in one minute What happens to your BCH when you die? If nobody has your keys, the coins are lost for good. If somebody has them, they can take everything today. Pusaka is a Bitcoin Cash wallet with the inheritance plan built in. Set it up once. Name your heirs and their shares (equal, your own split, or Islamic inheritance, faraid), three trusted contacts, a waiting time and a review period. Use it like any wallet. Send and receive, and swap on Chipnet (mainnet has no qualified pair yet). Every payment you send proves you are still here and restarts the waiting time. No reminders to press, unless you go a long time without paying anyone. If you go quiet, anyone can open a claim once the waiting time has passed, or two of your three contacts can open one sooner. The revised plans enforce the review period even when the owner pays the payout fee. Stop claim, or a payment you send, ends the claim and returns the plan to active use. After the review, anyone can press Pay the heirs. When the plan covers the network fee and every heir’s minimum payment, a visitor can submit the payout without a wallet. The same plan covers a lost key: if the owner can no longer sign, two contacts can open a claim, and the coins reach the people named instead of being lost. A second wallet of the owner's own can be one of them. No company holds the coins and no server stores the plan. Four SolidCash contracts do the work: the plan (PusakaAssetPlan) with its state in a CashTokens NFT, its receive address (PusakaV2Inbox), the review clock (PusakaV2ReviewAnchor, a BIP68 relative time lock) and a token vault (PusakaTokenVault) that keeps swapped tokens under the same rules.

title: The judge path: one minute, no wallet
text: The judge path: one minute, no wallet Do this What you should see You play the family of an owner who went quiet. Inheritance takes time by design: a waiting time, then a review the owner can use to stop the claim. So the demo starts near the end of a real plan, where those steps have already happened on mainnet, and leaves the last one to you. Do this What you should see Open the demo Pay out a real inheritance: what already happened, step by step. Plan created and Claim opened (each links to its transaction), Owner went quiet and Review ended (no transaction of their own, just time passing), then Your turn: pay the heirs Press Pay the heirs A review sheet listing each of the six heirs by name with their exact amount, then the network fee, paid from the plan. Nothing is sent yet Review the six payments, then press Send transaction "Transaction accepted by the network" with a View transaction link. The last step turns into Heirs paid Open View transaction One transaction, one output per heir: pot × share ÷ 120, rounded down Press Open the next example Another example plan, one with its payout ready whenever there is one Each example pays out once, so the demo keeps a pool of identical ones (four assets-2 examples, plus six earlier assets-1 ones as fallbacks) and opens one that is ready. title: The owner path: five minutes, with Paytaca or Cashonize
text: The owner path: five minutes, with Paytaca or Cashonize Open Create a plan and connect your wallet with the QR code (WizardConnect). Add heirs and their shares, then three trusted contacts. Use ordinary receive addresses (bitcoincash:q…). Tip: use other receive addresses of your own wallet, and every payout comes back to you. Choose the waiting time and the review period (at least a day each), and a starting amount. Review and approve in your wallet. If your coins are spread over several addresses, press Prepare wallet first: a separate transaction that gathers them at your first receive address. Save the plan link when the app asks. Then try Send (the waiting time moves forward), Receive and Collect, I'm still here, Edit inheritance rules, and Take available BCH back from the ⋯ menu. Every review sheet shows each output and fee before your wallet is asked to sign. The wallet signs only; the app broadcasts the exact transaction you reviewed and checks its ID.

title: The whole cycle yourself: about 30 minutes, on Chipnet
text: The whole cycle yourself: about 30 minutes, on Chipnet A plan you create on mainnet needs at least a day for each of the waiting time and the review, so that a short absence never costs an owner their savings. (The demo's examples were made by our script with a 1-minute wait.) To run every step yourself, use the quick test plan on Chipnet with test BCH from a Chipnet faucet: Create the plan as above, with Quick test ticked: a 1-minute waiting time and a 512-second review, the shortest the network can enforce. Wait for the waiting time to pass. The network clock moves with each block, so this takes a block or two. Press Open the claim on your plan. The review starts once the claim is confirmed in a block. When the review ends, press Pay the heirs. One transaction pays every heir. Expect about 20 to 30 minutes in all, depending on how quickly blocks arrive.

title: What the network refuses
text: What the network refuses Each row is checked by a test that builds the attacker's transaction and expects it to fail, under the BCH 2026 limits and a strict BIP68 verifier (contract/test/v2/). Someone tries to Result Test Pay out one second before the review ends Refused: the anchor is not old enough rejects backdated openClaim locktime, unconfirmed anchor, insufficient MTP shift, and elapsed = delay - 1s Pay out early with the owner paying the fee on the revised anchor Refused until BIP68 review matures keeps owner cancellation available and applies the same review time to an owner-sponsored payout Use owner cancellation to produce a paid, stale, or still-approved plan Refused by the revised anchor accepts cancellation only into the next ACTIVE round with cleared approvals Open a claim with a backdated time, or skip the review with a wrong sequence Refused rejects non-version-2 tx, disabled/height-mode/too-short sequence, and open+finalize in same tx Swap an heir's address, or use a fake or stale claim marker Refused rejects substituted, plain-BCH, wrong-plan, wrong-round anchors, repeated openClaim, and hijacked payout Vote twice as the same contact, replay a vote, forge the policy, or skim the receive address Refused rejects all adversarial attack vectors (fee-reserve siphon, contact double-vote/replay, substitution, policy forgery, CLTV bypass, inbox skim) Stop a claim without being the owner Refused; the owner's stop works and restarts the clock enforces owner cancelClaim (rejects stranger, stops old finalize after delay, restarts fresh round 2 delay, allows ownerWithdraw) Take part of the fee reserve as change while paying out Refused rejects a caller taking part of the review fee reserve as a self-funded change output Redirect a payment, forge the state NFT or overcharge a collection Refused rejects adversarial attacks: recipient substitution, container dust violation, backdated locktime regression, forged NFTs, inbox skimming, excessive self-sweep fee, double container merge, and token junk Swap through a fake pool, or with an expired quote Refused rejects expired quotes, fake pool scripts, zero minimum, wrong network metadata and old BCH-only plans And what must work: a review that both a contact quorum and inactivity must respect, ten heirs at once, money that arrives after a payout or after the owner left still reaching the heirs, and a fresh browser restoring a plan from its link. Run them yourself (Node 24): cd contract && npm install && npm test # all contract tests, v1 and v2 cd app && npm install && npm run build && npm run test:ui

title: Current limits
text: Current limits Earlier plan addresses. The app still opens plans created with the earlier review anchor and labels them. Those contracts allow an early payout signed and sponsored by the owner to the registered heirs. The revised anchor enforces the delay for owner-sponsored payouts on newly created assets-2 plans. Token inheritance after taking BCH back. Token payouts follow a completed BCH payout. If the owner takes back the available BCH and leaves tokens in the vault, the plan needs a BCH top-up before the heirs can claim them.

title: Good to know
text: Good to know Keep the plan link. Every claim and payout needs the plan's rules, which travel in the link after the # and never reach a server. Pusaka keeps no copy. The BCH stays safe in the contracts without the link, but nobody can act on it. Fees. Opening a claim and paying the heirs each cost about 4,000 to 5,000 satoshis, taken from the plan. Owner actions cost a similar fee from the owner's wallet or the plan. Pusaka takes no fee of its own today. The network clock runs about an hour behind. Plans follow the median time of the last 11 blocks, so every date in the app says "about". Up to 10 heirs, each with an ordinary BCH address, and each share at least 546 satoshis when paid. Faraid is worked out in the browser. The contracts enforce the resulting numbers, not the rules of faraid. It is not a legal will. It moves only the BCH and tokens held by the plan. More: README, the design rules, the SolidCash developer log and the feedback for SolidCash.

title: Inheritance wallet
text: How the wallet protects funds, receives payments, and handles claims. 17 November 2026. Original architecture selection and proof requirements. The resulting v2 implementation is described in the plan format and the verification record. The candidate constructions below preserve the reasoning and do not replace that current evidence. Product requirements are in PRODUCT.md. The current app and asset release are recorded here; the constructions below retain the original design investigation.

title: Constraints and existing evidence
text: Constraints and existing evidence The existing SolidCash contract has a shared deadline, fixed multi-heir payout and owner authorization through a co-spent ordinary P2PKH coin. Paytaca mobile approved a mainnet plan creation through the current WizardConnect bridge. The offline relay serialization tests pass. A complete new wallet flow has not been tested in Paytaca; creation is not proof of every signing capability. @wizardconnect/dapp in this app exposes transaction signing, not a portable arbitrary-message signing method. The protocol's optional extension mechanism does not imply Paytaca implements a proposed check-in or contact-signature API. The SDK uses state NFTs and separate balance containers. Its deployed target address and logical BCH balance are not interchangeable. A "Receive" button cannot simply expose getAddress() and assume arbitrary deposits become balance. Normal Paytaca coins have fixed P2PKH spending conditions. No monitor, pre-signed timer or xpub access changes their authorization rules. Avoid stale pre-signed transaction schemes that fail when the owner spends their inputs.

title: Candidate construction
text: Candidate construction Use an inheritance-aware BCH balance controlled by a single authenticated plan state. Keep Paytaca as the owner key holder; Pusaka builds the transactions and never requests a mnemonic or stores an owner spending key. A unique plan identity authenticates the current policy and state. Balance containers and any receive/inbox covenant must require that identity, the correct successor state and conservation of value. A matching token category alone is insufficient if unrelated NFTs or extra minting authority can forge the expected state role. send(destination, amount) requires fresh owner authorization. It reduces the logical balance by the approved payment and fees, preserves protected change and updates owner activity in the same transaction. It must work repeatedly. checkIn() is the small standalone owner transaction. Both it and send clear a pending claim and advance a round identifier. Require timestamp-based locktime, a non-final sequence and a non-decreasing deadline when using the existing absolute-deadline design; the caller-supplied locktime is not a trusted wall clock. The client uses fresh network time; stale authorization must not become a reusable future cancellation. A receive covenant or inbox accepts ordinary payments and binds them to this plan. The selection must prove independent incoming UTXOs, protected change, multiple deposits, dust, fresh-session discovery and post-claim receipts. If sweeping is necessary, it must not depend on a dead owner's signature. Do not assume an SDK method named deposit solves arbitrary incoming payments. Each contact has a configured identity. A transaction authorized by a contact records one approval for this plan, policy version and activity round. Distinct contacts count once. The quorum creates a Review state. An expired inactivity condition may also create Review without contact cooperation. Only after the complete review delay may an unrestricted submitter request the predetermined payout. Owner cancellation spends the same authenticated claim state, so its invalidation is enforced by consensus rather than an app flag. Keep the current Pusaka.scash and existing plan links readable as v1. Build v2 as a separate artifact and explicit plan version. Do not reuse the old artifact for a new policy or imply funded contracts are upgradeable.

title: Two immediate engineering gates
text: Two immediate engineering gates

title: A. Prove the wallet benefit before changing the screens
text: A. Prove the wallet benefit before changing the screens Start with a minimal partial-payment contract, the real SDK and the current external signer. Exercise: fund, pay part, retain change, receive again, pay again, and recover the plan from a new session. The present owner-co-spend pattern is a candidate authorization path because it uses ordinary wallet signing. Prove the required owner input and its change, including the case where nearly all owner funds are in Pusaka. Do not require a surprising second top-up before each payment. A small persistent owner coin or a different supported authorization route must have explicit fee accounting. Gate A passes only when funds remain covered after partial spending, new receipts have an enforceable claim path, and the real Paytaca request is understandable. A simulator-only send is useful evidence but does not pass the wallet gate.

title: B. Anchor the review delay to the actual claim transition
text: B. Anchor the review delay to the actual claim transition Do not implement reviewEndsAt = tx.locktime + reviewPeriod as the only protection. A hostile claimant can choose an old locktime, allowing a newly opened review to appear already finished. tx.time constrains the spending transaction's locktime; it does not supply an incorruptible "now" to store in state. Preferred candidate: create a dedicated authenticated claim UTXO on entry to Review. Finalization must consume it with a consensus-enforced relative time lock (OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, transaction version 2, time-based BIP68 encoding). The delay starts from that newly created output's chain age. Round the configured duration upward to 512-second units and explain network-time approximation. Require the specific claim anchor and reject substitutes. Owner cancellation consumes or invalidates it. Unauthenticated deposits and repeated votes must not recreate it, restart its age or advance the round. If the normal SDK state update always recreates the relevant UTXO, a separate claim covenant is necessary. Incoming funds during Review must either join without changing the anchor or remain in a safe inbox claimable by the same heirs; they must not need owner consent to join. The compiler, SDK input sequence handling, output identity and full transaction limits need an executable proof. The CashScript documentation currently notes a time-based sequence limitation in its transaction builder. Do not assume that language support alone proves the installed SolidCash path can build it. If it cannot, investigate a small dedicated covenant and lower-level builder; do not replace a seconds-based duration with a block count without revisiting semantics.

title: Authorization and convenience options
text: Authorization and convenience options Contact co-spend transactions can use ordinary wallet approvals, like the current owner path, subject to proving the contact is the authorized input in the relevant method. There is no need to invent a portable message API for the first version. checkDataSig makes signed statements a possible later construction on BCH. It does not make EIP-712 or WebAuthn signatures drop-in replacements. Prove the exact digest, signature format and wallet capability. Bind any signed message to the network, unique plan, policy version, action, activity round or claim identity and freshness condition. Reject a pre-claim message used to cancel a later claim. Relayers can pay fees and submit authorized actions. They must have no authority to redirect funds, fabricate life proofs or be required for the owner to stop a claim. Notifications and indexing may use a service, with direct chain access and portable plan data as fallback. "No server" is not a reason to remove useful UX. Passkey support needs a separate signature-verification and key-recovery design. Browser biometrics alone are not a BCH-verifiable owner authorization. Keep it outside the initial wallet proof rather than presenting a server decision as equivalent to the earlier on-chain passkey verification.

title: Assets and trading
text: Assets and trading The first wallet proof is BCH. A trading demonstration additionally needs one named adapter and fungible CashToken containers whose balances can be distributed under the same family policy. Token category, returned amount, protected change, slippage limits, fee payer and recipient must be bound into the approved transaction. An asset sitting in a pool, an order, a lending position or a custodial exchange is not automatically in the inheritable balance. Supporting positions requires a proved redemption/claim adapter, not just displaying their market value. Nonfungible assets require an explicit recipient rule; a percentage split cannot divide an NFT.

title: Required adversarial checks
text: Required adversarial checks Stranger cannot send, check in, change the policy or cancel a claim. Wrong or fabricated plan NFT cannot authorize balance spending or a receive sweep. Payee substitution, excessive fees and unprotected change are rejected. Incoming funds, repeated votes and self-transfers without owner authorization cannot renew life or indefinitely delay a valid claim. Same contact twice, another plan's approval and a previous round's approval do not satisfy the quorum. Backdated opening locktime, same-transaction opening/finalization, wrong anchor, disabled/wrong-unit sequence and early finalization cannot bypass the review delay. An owner action invalidates the old anchor and all old approvals; an old message cannot stop a later claim. Concurrent owner and payout submissions resolve through the authenticated state; neither UI assumes success before chain confirmation. Every heir gets the configured share of the latest covered balance; rounding, token amounts, carrier values, dust and fee reserves are accounted for. Empty balances, deposits during Review and deposits after a payout have defined, recoverable spending paths. No old receive address strands future funds. Lost relay session and a fresh browser can recover the same plan using public metadata and the owner's wallet, without storing a private spending key.

title: Sources
text: Sources EIP-7702: delegation changes account code on supporting EVM chains; it is not a BCH wallet feature. BCH model and covenants: spending conditions, introspection and constrained change outputs. Time locks: tx.time, tx.locktime, this.age, sequence encoding and builder limitations. Signature checks: transaction signatures and checkDataSig are separate verification mechanisms. WizardConnect protocol and extensions: transaction signing is the base interaction; extra capabilities require wallet support.

title: Plan format
text: Plan links, policy commitments, and on-chain state. Date: 17 November 2026 Status: Stage 3 Specification & SDK Schema (contract/scripts/v2/pusaka-v2.ts) This document defines the versioned off-chain metadata schema (pusaka-v2) and on-chain binary layouts for Pusaka v2. Legacy version: 1 (pusaka-v1 / Pusaka.scash) links and deployed plans remain completely separate and unmodified.

title: 1. Design Principles
text: 1. Design Principles Cycle-Free Covenant DAG: PusakaV2Anchor.scash: constructor (planCategory, ownerPkh) -> reads reviewSequence dynamically from its 8-byte none-NFT commitment (bytes4(round) || bytes4(reviewSequence)) and authenticates input 0 via planCategory + 0x02. PusakaV2Plan.scash: constructor (planCategory, ownerPkh, anchorLockingBytecode) -> holds the unique minting NFT (planCategory + 0x02) and all protected BCH directly. Mutable policy (heirs, contacts, inactivityPeriod, reviewSequence, feeBudget) is committed by policyHash = hash256(policyBytes) inside the 51-byte NFT commitment rather than baked into constructor args. PusakaV2Inbox.scash: constructor (planCategory, planLockingBytecode, perInputFeeCap) -> derives a single long-lived ordinary P2SH32 receive address (inboxAddress) that never changes across owner policy edits, partial spends, claim reviews, exits, or payouts. No Stranded Funds & Post-Exit Protection (CLOSED): Owner full spendable drains, ownerExit() (CLOSED), and finalizeClaim()/distributeLate() (PAID_OUT) always preserve a >= 1,000-satoshi Plan minting-NFT carrier so inboxAddress remains continuously sweepable and recoverable. CLOSED (0x03) represents a withdrawn/retired balance with the long-lived inboxAddress still active. ownerExit() is timestamp-authenticated (tx.time >= 500000000) and renews deadline = max(curDeadline, tx.locktime + period) (bounded <= 4294967295). Any post-exit receipts swept into CLOSED remain owner-recoverable (ownerExit() / checkIn()) AND retain both inheritance paths (openClaimByInactivity() after deadline and 2-of-3 contactApprove() quorum) whenever spendable funds exist (tx.inputs[0].value > 1000). A 1st contact vote preserves CLOSED without silently reactivating the plan; only 2-contact quorum or expired inactivity enters REVIEW and mints a fresh PusakaV2Anchor for a full reviewSequence delay. Sweeps into CLOSED never renew deadline or reset votes. (Reaching zero balance via ownerExit() retires the current balance, not a promise to disable future receipts at the old inboxAddress from following the family plan.) Bounded Owner Fee Funding: Owner actions (send, checkIn, cancelClaim, updatePolicy) require an authenticated ownerPkh co-spend (inputs[1] or inputs[2] during REVIEW) committing to the transaction, and allow up to 10,000 sats (MAX_OWNER_TX_FEE) of network fee to be drawn from protected BCH above the 1,000-sat carrier (outputs[0].value >= max(1000, nextPlanSats - 10000)). Non-plan change outputs cannot draw on protected funds (change <= extraIn) and, whenever any fee is taken from protected funds, change must return to ownerLock. A small persistent ordinary authorization coin (e.g. 600 sats) can therefore be returned intact across repeated owner actions without repeated ordinary-wallet top-ups. SDK builders accept ownerUtxos?: Utxo[] (and ownerUtxo?: Utxo) with feeFunding?: 'auto' | 'owner' | 'protected', preserving legacy owner-funded behavior in 'auto' when ordinary coins leave >= 546 sats change and otherwise using protected/hybrid fees so the owner auth coin is not silently burned.

title: App and assets
text: Evidence for token receipts, swaps, and phone signing. The first asset release (assets-1) proved swaps and token payouts on Chipnet and Paytaca phone signing. The revised anchor (assets-2) binds owner cancellation to a new active round and applies the review period to owner-sponsored payouts. The BCH lifecycle records are in v2-live.md.

title: Application
text: Application Published app: https://astrorehan.github.io/pusaka-bch/ (mainnet) and https://astrorehan.github.io/pusaka-bch/chipnet/ (Chipnet). Example plans: /wallet/demo on either. The desktop sidebar folds into a rail. Phones use a drawer. Wallet, inheritance, activity, setup and swap are separate routes. Transaction dialogs show recipients, fees, protected change and returned authorization funds before signing. app/src/lib/protocol/ contains the browser-safe codecs, artifacts and builders. The contract runner re-exports the same module. No filesystem loaders, test keys, mnemonics or chain runners enter the client bundle. npm run check:artifacts compares all six bundled artifacts with compiler output. The app discovers live plan/inbox/token UTXOs and uses confirmed-anchor chain age for review readiness. It checks for stale plan state before signing. Wallet rejection, quote expiry and ambiguous broadcast failure are explicit outcomes. Local activity records say Accepted, not confirmed. Explorer links let users inspect confirmations; importing a plan does not pretend to import its history. Onboarding keeps an ordinary owner coin of at least 600 sats, separate from the 1,000-sat plan identity. A separately reviewed preparation transaction can gather ordinary HD wallet coins into the first receive address. Each owner action still requires normal wallet approval. A plan link or JSON restores public state without holding a spending key. Saved browser data is a convenience, not the sole backup. /plan and /legacy/new retain the v1 code path. New setup at /new and /wallet/new creates the asset-enabled revision. Existing contracts do not upgrade.

title: Asset revision
text: Asset revision The first asset release retained version: pusaka-v2 and added protocolRevision: assets-1. Missing revision selects the original v2 artifact. Unknown revisions fail closed. The new PusakaAssetPlan retains the prior state machine and adds: assetAction(maximumDebit): owner co-signature, bounded approved BCH debit, identity preservation, deadline renewal, round advancement and review cancellation. assetDistribution(): a public co-spend of a PAID_OUT plan that preserves its complete state and BCH. It lets the token covenant authenticate the current policy. PusakaTokenVault binds the immutable plan identity and locking script. An owner token send co-spends the plan, renewing activity. Public token payout requires a completed BCH claim and the current policy preimage. Old policy links cannot redirect a payout. Token carriers and payout fees come from the submitter's ordinary BCH, while the plan and receipt BCH remain preserved. Fungible amounts use integer floor shares. All indivisible rounding units go to the final configured heir. A tiny receipt may give zero token units to earlier heirs; their carrier outputs remain plain BCH. No token units are burned or left as an unclaimable remainder. NFTs and arbitrary DeFi positions are outside this flow.

title: Supported swap
text: Supported swap The supported pair is BCH / PSK on Chipnet, using a real Cauldron V0 pool. PSK is a test fungible token with no monetary value. Mainnet trading stays unavailable until a real pair and phone signing have been qualified. The adapter uses @cashlab/cauldron to derive the actual pool script and unlocker. It verifies that the configured pool address matches that script, reconstructs the pool at its input index, applies the pool's 0.3% liquidity fee and checks a positive minimum return. Quotes expire after 60 seconds. A conflicting pool spend invalidates the whole transaction. The owner's signature commits to exact outputs. One atomic swap spends protected BCH, renews activity, returns the ordinary auth coin, recreates the pool and pays fungible proceeds directly to the token vault. There is no intermediate unprotected owner token output or separate allocation. The UI supports BCH-to-token purchase for this pair, not arbitrary pairs or sales. Protocol reference: https://docs.riftenlabs.com/cauldron/swap/

title: 1. Stateful calls cannot be signed by an outside wallet (fixed with a patch)
text: 1. Stateful calls cannot be signed by an outside wallet (fixed with a patch) What happened. A web app cannot hold keys, so every transaction must be signed by the user's wallet over bch_signTransaction, the request WizardConnect carries. The SDK has Signer.external({ wallet, address, publicKey }) for this. Deploy works as shipped. Every stateful call failed: The message-bus path (.call.checkIn().send()) runs evaluateEveryInput in dist/message-bus/preflight.js while the wallet's input still holds its all-zero placeholder signature, so it stops with preflight failed at input 2 (OP_VERIFY without the public key, NULLFAIL with it). With the preflight skipped for that input, the node refused the broadcast: Signature must be zero for failed CHECK(MULTI)SIG. dist/stateful/stb-submit-final-transaction.js broadcasts the placeholder bytes. TransactionBuilder.send and the framed call path call applyExternalSignatures; the stateful message-bus path never does. Reproduction. contract/scripts/external-signing-spike.ts: the whole lifecycle on Chipnet with only the SDK (ContractFactory, StatefulContract) and a stand-in wallet that signs exactly what bch_signTransaction hands it. Without the patch, the first checkIn fails as above. Impact. Any dapp whose users sign in their own wallet (Paytaca, Cashonize, any WizardConnect wallet) cannot call a stateful function. For Pusaka it blocked I'm still here, take back and send to heirs. Our fix (the patch, about 20 lines in two files): In evaluateEveryInput, skip an input whose unlocker is externally signed while it still holds the placeholder. Our reasoning: no covenant reads another input's unlocking bytecode, so that input can be judged after signing. In sendPreflightedMessageBusTransaction, call applyExternalSignatures first and then judge every input on the signed bytes. In submitFinalTransaction, call applyExternalSignatures before the bytes are broadcast. The placeholder has the signature's size, so the fee does not change. After the patch, on Chipnet: I'm still here cf6ffd83…1c80, take back 62dfa7e0…3d1a, and a payout to 6 heirs paid by a stranger's wallet 187ac296…a90c. Suggested upstream fix. Take the patch as a PR. One change worth making on the way: our patch spots the placeholder by its bytes (a 65-byte push of zeros); upstream could mark it on the unlocker instead.

title: 2. A payout loop cannot be combined with a time check
text: 2. A payout loop cannot be combined with a time check What happened. Two separate failures, both with a timestamp locktime on the call: When the SDK derives the outputs, any function that reads tx.time or tx.locktime and transfers fails with VM failed at ip 14 opcode 82 (OP_VERIFY). Our guess, not checked: the derivation run does not use the call's locktime. With explicit .transfer() outputs, the preflight fails whenever the transfers come from a loop: messageBus: BCH-2026 preflight failed at input 0: Program failed an OP_VERIFY operation. So a time-locked payout needs explicit outputs, and explicit outputs need unrolled transfers. Reproduction. Two payees, mock network with the real 2026 limits: pragma solidcash ^0.50.0; contract ReproLoop(int deadline) { bytes20[] public payees; constructor(bytes20[] initialPayees) { this.payees = initialPayees; } function payAll() public { // fails, derived or explicit outputs require(tx.time >= deadline); int each = (this.balance - 2000) / int(this.payees.length); for (int i = 0; i < int(this.payees.length); i++) { this.transfer(new LockingBytecodeP2PKH(this.payees[i]), each); } } function payTwoUnrolled() public { // works only with explicit outputs require(tx.time >= deadline); int each = (this.balance - 2000) / 2; this.transfer(new LockingBytecodeP2PKH(this.payees[0]), each); this.transfer(new LockingBytecodeP2PKH(this.payees[1]), each); } } Call each with .setLocktime(t) (with t just below the mock's latest time), once letting the SDK derive the outputs and once with .transfer(lock, each) per payee: Function body Outputs Result loop of this.transfer, no time check derived OK same, with .setLocktime(t) on the call derived OK same explicit preflight failure (OP_VERIFY) require(tx.time >= deadline) + loop derived VM failed at ip 14 require(tx.time >= deadline) + loop explicit preflight failure require(tx.time >= deadline) after the loop derived VM failed at ip 14 require(tx.locktime >= deadline) + loop derived VM failed at ip 14 require(tx.time >= deadline) + two unrolled transfers derived VM failed at ip 14 require(tx.time >= deadline) + two unrolled transfers explicit OK The contract above and the nine cases in the table are the complete reproduction. Impact. Any contract that pays a list of people after a date: wills, vesting, payroll, escrow with many parties. Pusaka uses ten guarded slots (if (i < len) this.transfer(...)) and caps heirs at 10. Suggested fix. Use the call's locktime in the derivation run, and let the preflight accept transfers emitted from a loop when the explicit outputs match. If loops are out of scope for now, a compiler error that names the limit would save a day.

title: 3. npx solidhat test on Windows passes without running any test
text: 3. npx solidhat test on Windows passes without running any test What happened. On Windows, npx solidhat test prints the compile lines and exits with code 0, without running a single test. npx vitest run -c vitest.solidhat.config.ts runs them. Reproduction. Any SolidHat TypeScript project on Windows 11 with Node 24.11; ours is contract/. Impact. A green result with no tests behind it; a CI job on Windows would pass the same way. We noticed only because the output had no test lines. Suggested fix. Find why the test runner does not start on Windows (a path or spawn issue is our guess, not checked). Until then, exit non-zero when no test file ran. Our workaround: "test": "solidhat compile && vitest run -c vitest.solidhat.config.ts" in package.json.

title: 4. Memory-aliasing error on a common Solidity struct pattern
text: 4. Memory-aliasing error on a common Solidity struct pattern What happened. The Monad project's FaraidLib.sol (230 lines of Solidity 0.8.24: structs, enums, custom errors, exact fractions) compiles unchanged as a library, which was a good surprise. Calling FaraidLib.compute() from a contract fails: "Memory alias group 'pool, factor' reaches an operation that cannot yet preserve Solidity aliasing". Reproduction (evmCompat: true): pragma solidity ^0.8.24; contract AliasB { struct Frac { uint256 num; uint256 den; } function add(Frac memory a, Frac memory b) internal pure returns (Frac memory) { return Frac(a.num * b.den + b.num * a.den, a.den * b.den); } function check(uint256 x) public pure { Frac memory pool = Frac(x, 2); Frac memory factor = add(pool, Frac(1, 3)); // error: alias group 'pool, factor' require(factor.num > 0); } } Passing a local memory struct into an internal function that returns a memory struct is enough; no reassignment is needed. Passing only temporaries (add(Frac(x, 2), Frac(1, 3))) compiles. Impact. Fraction and math libraries use this pattern everywhere, so it blocks a lot of EVM code from porting. For us it blocked checking faraid on chain; the shares are computed in the browser instead. Suggested fix. Copy the struct when aliasing cannot be proven safe for a pure function, or at least point the error at the call site and suggest the temporary-only form.

title: 5. The template's mock uses relaxed limits
text: 5. The template's mock uses relaxed limits What happened. The mock's default consensus limits are relaxed (1 MB inputs, 1 MB NFT commitments, no dust check). The README says so, but the TypeScript template keeps the relaxed mock. Reproduction. A new project from the TypeScript template: its solidcash.config.ts has no consensus block. Impact. A new project's green tests say little about whether its transactions are valid on chain. Stateful calls are large (ours are 9 to 12 KB), so the gap matters. Suggested fix. Make the real limits the template default. Ours, with which all 58 of our tests pass: mock: { type: 'mock', consensus: { maximumInputBytes: 10_000, maximumStackItemBytes: 10_000, maximumTransactionBytes: 1_000_000, maximumNftCommitmentBytes: 128, }, policy: { enforceDust: true }, },

title: 6. initialState is silently ignored for a dynamic struct array
text: 6. initialState is silently ignored for a dynamic struct array What happened. initialState: { heirs: [...] } for a Heir[] state variable is ignored with no message; the state comes back as []. Passing the array through a constructor(Heir[] initialHeirs) works. Reproduction. Deploy Pusaka with initialState: { heirs: [...] } instead of the constructor argument, then read getState(). Impact. Wrong state with no error. We lost time before trying the constructor. Suggested fix. Support it, or throw an error that names the field and suggests the constructor.

title: 7. Re-attaching to a deployed stateful contract is undocumented
text: 7. Re-attaching to a deployed stateful contract is undocumented What happened. An app that reloads a plan from a saved link must rebuild the contract object. ContractFactory.attach(category) alone fails with "Expected 4 arguments". What works: new StatefulContract(new Contract(artifact, [ownerPkh, period, total, feeBudget], { provider }), categoryId) The category is not the genesis txid but the txid of the coin the genesis spends first (deployed.categoryId). Passing the genesis txid gives "Expected 1 data NFT(s) ... found 0". Reproduction. Deploy any stateful contract with constructor arguments, then attach with the genesis txid. Impact. Every app that reloads a contract after a page reload or on another device. Suggested fix. attach(category, constructorArgs) on the factory, a docs page on re-attaching, and an error that says "this looks like a genesis txid; pass the category id".

title: 8. A stateful call wants 11 separate coins from the caller
text: 8. A stateful call wants 11 separate coins from the caller What happened. distribute (about 12 KB, 16 inputs) asks for 11 separate plain coins from the caller. With none, it fails with Signer has 0 available plain UTXO(s) but 11 funder(s) needed. A wallet holding one coin is first asked to sign a split into 11. The SDK also swept several of the caller's small change coins into the payout. Reproduction. Call distribute on a 6-heir Pusaka from a wallet that holds one coin. Impact. A visitor pressing "Send to heirs" signs twice, and pays for more inputs than needed. Suggested fix. Can the funder count be lower? If not, document why, and expose the count before the call so an app can prepare the coins in one step.

title: 9. No helper for the network's time on a live network
text: 9. No helper for the network's time on a live network What happened. A timestamp locktime is final only below the median time past of the last 11 blocks. SolidHat scripts have no time.latest() on a live network, so our script reads the last 11 block headers over Electrum (blockchain.block.header) and takes the median. Chipnet's median time past was 4,449 seconds (about 74 minutes) behind the clock on 15 Nov. Reproduction. Call any function guarded by tx.time with setLocktime(Date.now() / 1000) on Chipnet: the node refuses the transaction as not final. Impact. Every contract that uses tx.time. Without the helper, calls fail, or deadlines land an hour off. Suggested fix. provider.getMedianTimePast() in the SDK, and a docs line next to tx.time about the lag.

title: 10. An early time-locked call shows the locktime error, not the contract's
text: 10. An early time-locked call shows the locktime error, not the contract's What happened. A distribute before the deadline fails with the CLTV locktime message, not the contract's custom error or require message, because the transaction's locktime check fails first. Reproduction. Test nobody can distribute before the deadline in contract/test/Pusaka.test.ts; it can only assert that the call fails. Impact. Developers and users see a consensus message instead of the reason they wrote. Suggested fix. When a call fails on locktime, say which tx.time or tx.locktime check it relates to.

title: 11. solidhat compile silently skips subfolders of contracts/
text: 11. solidhat compile silently skips subfolders of contracts/ What happened. Only .scash files directly inside contracts/ are compiled. A file in contracts/repro/ was skipped with no message, and the test then failed with "no SolidCash artifact named ...". We did not check whether a config option exists. Impact. Hardhat compiles subfolders, so ported projects expect it. Suggested fix. Compile subfolders, or warn about .scash files that were skipped.

title: 12. bytes.length is uint256 under evmCompat
text: 12. bytes.length is uint256 under evmCompat What happened. Porting our CashScript prototype needed one change besides the pragma: with evmCompat: true (the template default), int n = heirs.length / 24; fails with "Type 'uint256' can not be assigned to variable of type 'int256'". The fix is int n = int(heirs.length) / 24;. Impact. Not a bug, but it is the first error most CashScript users will hit when porting. Suggested fix. Suggest the cast in the error message.

title: 13. Noisy messages
text: 13. Noisy messages STB debug() best-effort error: Cannot debug a transaction with custom unlocker is printed on every wallet-signed call. It is harmless but reads like a failure. Suggest printing it only in debug mode. tx.origin gives a warning recommending checkSig. For our one require (line 28, inside a modifier used by two functions) solidhat compile printed it four times. Suggest one warning per source location, and a docs note on when co-spending an owner coin is the right pattern: it lets any wallet authorise a call by signing only its own ordinary coin.

title: 14. Smaller gaps
text: 14. Smaller gaps ElectrumNetworkProvider has no getBalance; we sum getUtxos(address). Signer.external names one address, while WizardConnect is an HD session (xpubs) whose wallets move change to new addresses. A contract that checks the owner's address then needs the app to gather the coins there first. Support for an HD signer (WizardConnect's inputPaths) would remove that step. The GitHub master branch reports 0.14.0-beta.1 in its package.json files while npm has 0.50.x (published 7 Nov), so the docs in the repo may describe an older release. npm create @solidcash/solidhat@0.50.0 contract fails on Windows with ECOMPROMISED: Lock compromised. The error comes from npm's own npm exec lock (libnpmexec/lib/with-lock.js, npm 11.6.2), not from SolidHat. Workaround: install @solidcash/create-solidhat into a scratch folder and run its dist/cli.js with --template typescript --package-manager npm --yes. A line in the README would help Windows users. The TypeScript template's sample test only checks that a factory loads. A sample that sends a transaction and asserts a rejection would show new users the testing loop. For CashScript users: MockNetworkProvider moved to @solidcash/solidcash/network/mock, and addUtxo is now async. Worth a line in a migration note.

title: Q. Four 1,000-sat outputs locked with OP_1 in each payout
text: Q. Four 1,000-sat outputs locked with OP_1 in each payout A question, not a report. Both of our distribute transactions on Chipnet (d76ffee1…25ad and 187ac296…a90c) have four outputs (#9 to #12) of 1,000 sats each whose locking bytecode is a single OP_1. Our checkIn transaction has none. A locking script of OP_1 can be spent by anyone. Are these intended (for example, swept by a later step), and could the docs say what they are for?

title: What worked well
text: What worked well The Solidity features we wanted all compiled: a struct, a struct array in state, a modifier, events, a custom error and the satoshi container (this.balance, this.transfer). The prototype compiled after one cast, and FaraidLib.sol compiled unchanged as a library. The SDK is close to CashScript (Contract, TransactionBuilder, SignatureTemplate, randomUtxo). The mock enforces BIP68 relative locktimes, which CashScript's mock did not. It caught a test of ours that had passed for a coin that was not old enough. The stateful contract ran its whole lifecycle on Chipnet with no change.

title: Developer log
text: The dated development record behind the feedback. A dated log of porting Pusaka (an inheritance contract first written in Solidity for Monad) to Bitcoin Cash with SolidCash during BCH BLAZE 2026. What was easy, what broke, workarounds, and links to issues or pull requests. Versions: @solidcash/solidhat 0.50.0, @solidcash/solidc 0.50.0, @solidcash/solidcash 0.50.1, Node 24.11, Windows 11.

title: 15 Nov 2026
text: 15 Nov 2026 Project setup npm create @solidcash/solidhat@0.50.0 contract failed on Windows with ECOMPROMISED: Lock compromised, also with a fresh npm cache. The error comes from npm's own npm exec lock (libnpmexec/lib/with-lock.js, npm 11.6.2), not from SolidHat. Workaround: install @solidcash/create-solidhat into a scratch folder and run node <that folder>/node_modules/@solidcash/create-solidhat/dist/cli.js contract --template typescript --package-manager npm --yes. Worth a line in the README for Windows users. The GitHub repository's master branch reports version 0.14.0-beta.1 in its package.json files, while npm has 0.50.x (published 7 Nov). The docs in the repo may therefore describe an older release than the one installed. The TypeScript template's sample (Counter) and test are minimal: the test only checks that a factory loads. A sample that sends a transaction and asserts a rejection would show new users the testing loop. Porting the CashScript prototype The stateless prototype (../prototype/vault.cash, CashScript 0.14) compiled after changing the pragma to pragma solidcash ^0.50.0; and one line: with evmCompat: true (the template's default), bytes.length is uint256, so int n = heirs.length / 24; fails with "Type 'uint256' can not be assigned to variable of type 'int256'". Fix: int n = int(heirs.length) / 24;. Not a bug, but CashScript users porting code will hit it first; the error could suggest the cast. The SDK API matches CashScript closely (Contract, TransactionBuilder, SignatureTemplate, randomUtxo). MockNetworkProvider moved to the subpath @solidcash/solidcash/network/mock, and addUtxo is now async. Good surprise: SolidCash's MockNetworkProvider enforces BIP68 relative locktimes (non-BIP68-final), which CashScript's mock did not. Our prototype test had passed for a coin that was not actually old enough. The port now mines the waiting period with provider.mine(n) before the payout, and a new test proves a check-in really resets the timer. All 12 prototype cases plus that one pass. Compiling the original Monad contracts (evmCompat) FaraidLib.sol (230 lines of plain Solidity 0.8.24: structs, enums, custom errors, exact fractions) compiles unchanged as a library. Calling FaraidLib.compute() from a contract fails: "Memory alias group 'pool, factor' reaches an operation that cannot yet preserve Solidity aliasing" at Frac memory pool = add(add(s.mother, s.father), s.daughters); inside _radd. Minimal reproduction (fails the same way; evmCompat: true): pragma solidity ^0.8.24; contract AliasB { struct Frac { uint256 num; uint256 den; } function add(Frac memory a, Frac memory b) internal pure returns (Frac memory) { return Frac(a.num * b.den + b.num * a.den, a.den * b.den); } function check(uint256 x) public pure { Frac memory pool = Frac(x, 2); Frac memory factor = add(pool, Frac(1, 3)); // error: alias group 'pool, factor' require(factor.num > 0); } } Passing a local memory struct into an internal function that returns a memory struct is enough; reassignment is not needed. Passing only temporaries (add(Frac(x, 2), Frac(1, 3))) compiles. This is a common Solidity pattern (fraction and math libraries), so it blocks a lot of EVM code. To report upstream as an issue with this reproduction. Stateful version (contracts/Pusaka.scash) Written in Solidity style: a struct Heir, a Heir[] state array, a deadline state variable, a modifier for the owner check, events, a custom error, and the satoshi container (this.balance, this.transfer). Compiles with evmCompat on. 11 tests pass in solidhat: check-in moves the deadline, strangers are refused, nobody can pay out early, a check-in on day 29 keeps the heirs waiting, all 6 faraid heirs are paid exactly in one transaction, 1-satoshi underpayment and a swapped address are refused, 10 heirs work, 11 are refused, withdraw empties the vault. Owner check without a signature in the contract input: require(tx.origin == new LockingBytecodeP2PKH(ownerPkh)). tx.origin is the first P2PKH input without tokens, so the owner's wallet only signs its own ordinary coin. Compiles with a warning on every read. Time in seconds: checkIn sets deadline = tx.locktime + period (with require(tx.locktime >= 500000000) so the locktime is a timestamp), and distribute requires tx.time >= this.deadline. Nothing is counted in blocks, so the May 2027 one-minute-block upgrade does not change the waiting period. A payout loop cannot be combined with a time check. Reduced to contracts/ReproLoop.scash and test/repro/loop-transfers.test.ts (two payees, mock network, real limits): Function body Outputs Result for loop of this.transfer, no time check derived by the SDK OK same, .setLocktime(t) on the call derived OK same explicit .transfer() calls messageBus: BCH-2026 preflight failed at input 0: Program failed an OP_VERIFY operation require(tx.time >= deadline) + loop derived VM failed at ip 14 opcode 82 (OP_VERIFY) require(tx.time >= deadline) + loop explicit preflight failure as above require(tx.time >= deadline) after the loop derived VM failed at ip 14 require(tx.locktime >= deadline) + loop derived VM failed at ip 14 require(tx.time >= deadline) + two unrolled this.transfer derived VM failed at ip 14 require(tx.time >= deadline) + two unrolled this.transfer explicit OK So two separate problems: (1) when the SDK derives the outputs, any function that reads tx.time or tx.locktime and transfers fails early (ip 14), perhaps because the derivation run does not use the call's locktime (guess); (2) explicit .transfer() outputs fail the preflight whenever the transfers come from a loop. A time-locked payout therefore needs explicit outputs, which need unrolled transfers. Pusaka uses ten guarded slots (if (i < len) this.transfer(...)) and caps heirs at 10. To report upstream with this table. initialState: { heirs: [...] } is silently ignored for a dynamic struct array (state comes back []); passing the array through a constructor(Heir[] ...) works. A warning or error would save time. An early distribute fails with the CLTV locktime message, not the contract's custom error, because the transaction's locktime check fails first. npx solidhat test on Windows prints the compile lines and exits 0 without running any test. npx vitest run -c vitest.solidhat.config.ts runs them. The mock's default consensus limits are relaxed (1 MB inputs, 1 MB NFT commitments, no dust check). The README says so, but the TypeScript template keeps the relaxed mock, so a new project's green tests say little about chain validity. We set the mock to the real 2026 limits (10,000-byte inputs and stack items, 128-byte commitments, dust enforced) in solidcash.config.ts; all tests still pass. Suggest making the strict limits the template default. Measured under those limits: distribute to 10 heirs is a 12,077-byte transaction with 16 inputs (master NFT, data NFTs, array chunks, satoshi container, caller's coin), about 12,000 satoshis in fees at 1 sat/byte. The caller's own coin pays the fee. First run on Chipnet (contract/scripts/chipnet-flow.ts, 15 Nov, about 06:51-06:54 UTC) The whole lifecycle ran on the real Chipnet network through SolidHat's Electrum provider, with no change to the contract: Step Transaction Size Vault A deployed (20,000 sats, 6 heirs) 993866968a678b289f1b2a9a5cd0f779f8114c8ea333a4cf7b4d519b7704c38d Owner check-in, deadline moved to locktime + 30 days 73dabfc17d3804fb6a6351a60885a07764c0cf0075fbd2d86c0195c3e34f2a12 9,209 bytes Owner withdraw, container left at 0 f3224bea4dc84c83ac3cd37e678b8088df4c85ab364e2895d853e7308df4a439 9,085 bytes Vault B deployed with its deadline an hour behind the network clock (60,000 sats) 3cb2d009d793c3e4bc75c14228461f61a60ea7fb3fd8099c0de01f604ad4956d Payout to all 6 faraid heirs, each exactly pot × share ÷ 120 d76ffee1296a7d11cc94719e696ed57cdd8781a1389f7fda71eaa66ad48e25ad 11,896 bytes, 16 inputs, 17 outputs, fee 12,086 sats (1.02 sat/byte) Chipnet's median time past was 4,449 seconds (about 74 minutes) behind the clock. A timestamp locktime must be below it, so a check-in sets the deadline about an hour earlier than "now + period". The app should say so, or add the lag to the period. The SolidHat scripts have no time.latest() on a live network; the script reads the last 11 block headers over Electrum (blockchain.block.header) and takes the median. A helper for this in the SDK would help anyone using tx.time. Fees: each stateful call is 9-12 KB, about 9,000-12,000 sats at 1 sat/byte, paid from the caller's own coins (the SDK also swept several of the caller's small change coins into the payout transaction). Wallet signing for stateful calls (contract/scripts/external-signing-spike.ts, 16 Nov, about 03:16-03:28 UTC) The web app cannot hold keys, so every transaction must be signed by the user's wallet over bch_signTransaction (the request WizardConnect also carries). The SDK has Signer.external({ wallet, address, publicKey }) for this. The spike runs the whole lifecycle on Chipnet with only the SDK (ContractFactory, StatefulContract) and a stand-in wallet that signs exactly what the protocol hands it. Deploy works as shipped. Two wallet requests: a 185-byte coin split, then the 952-byte genesis. Every stateful call failed before the fix. The message bus path (.call.checkIn().send()) judges every input in preflight.js while the wallet's input still holds its all-zero placeholder, so it stopped with preflight failed at input 2 (OP_VERIFY without the public key, NULLFAIL with it). With the preflight fixed, the node refused the broadcast (Signature must be zero for failed CHECK(MULTI)SIG), because stb-submit-final-transaction.js broadcasts the placeholder bytes. TransactionBuilder.send and the framed call path call applyExternalSignatures; the stateful message-bus path never does. Fix (contract/patches/@solidcash+solidcash+0.50.1.patch, applied with patch-package): skip a wallet input in evaluateEveryInput while it still holds the placeholder, and call applyExternalSignatures in submitFinalTransaction (and in sendPreflightedMessageBusTransaction) before the bytes go out. The placeholder has the signature's size, so the fee is unchanged. Reported upstream with the patch and a regression test: https://github.com/solidcash/solidcash/issues/3 (an issue, not a PR, because the public master has no 0.50 code). After the fix, all on Chipnet through the wallet: Step Transaction Wallet request I'm still here (deadline moved by exactly the period) cf6ffd83dc7fed321ed158ad40416dec90b2c176c6429233dab40b95e0381c80 3 inputs, wallet signs 1 Take back 62dfa7e0e090357643fcf6e832bfdcbeb2669dd0360150cf46adaec711793d1a 3 inputs, wallet signs 1 Send to 6 heirs, paid by a stranger's wallet 187ac29671c0c75ff40fdf9ab0ceb421f3e08e53e9167173402b62290d13a90c 16 inputs, wallet signs 11 Attach from a link needs the static constructor arguments and the category: new StatefulContract(new Contract(artifact, [ownerPkh, period, total, feeBudget], { provider }), categoryId). ContractFactory.attach(category) alone fails ("Expected 4 arguments"). The category is not the genesis txid but the txid of the coin the genesis spends first (deployed.categoryId); passing the genesis txid gives "Expected 1 data NFT(s) ... found 0". distribute wants 11 separate coins from the caller. A wallet with one coin is first asked to sign a split into 11 (Signer has 0 available plain UTXO(s) but 11 funder(s) needed when it has none). So a visitor pressing "Send to heirs" signs twice. Worth asking whether the funder count can be lower. STB debug() best-effort error: Cannot debug a transaction with custom unlocker is printed on every wallet-signed call. Harmless, but it reads like a failure. ElectrumNetworkProvider has no getBalance; sum getUtxos(address). WizardConnect (@wizardconnect/dapp 0.2.x) carries the same WcSignTransactionRequest plus inputPaths: [inputIndex, "receive" | "change", addressIndex], and the relay chunks large messages. It is an HD session (xpubs), while Signer.external and the contract's owner check name one address. An HD wallet moves change to new addresses, so the app must keep the owner's coins at the plan's owner address or consolidate them there before a call. The upstream form of the fix on Chipnet (16 Nov, about 05:14-05:17 UTC) The fix prepared for upstream (D:/project/lomba/solidcash-upstream, branch fix/external-signer-stateful-calls: rebuilt 0.50.1 sources, the fix, and 4 regression tests) was compiled, swapped into the published dist with our patch removed, and run through external-signing-spike.ts on Chipnet: deploy abacf5dee5eee019da552d549ef52f13d04928f9b35001218c37b1b15d8a9969, check-in f88794544ba68b4b91373943f2c3a0900a493dddbd918e6706f6e58ac3935b92 (deadline moved by exactly the period), withdraw 9e08246c0b5b26c50e7fbddedb94cfd9d54294f6dbde70eb1cd81fd267bab941, payout by another wallet a212685bd010dd1fa19d3b782cd6dbfccc3efcebbc2ffdd36197a690d53066b0. The SDK's default Chipnet Electrum server (chipnet.bch.ninja) dropped or timed out several connections during the run; chipnet.imaginary.cash worked (the spike takes ELECTRUM_HOST). The app's own chain layer on Chipnet (app/scripts/chain-e2e.ts, 16 Nov, about 03:42-03:48 UTC) The web app's src/lib/chain code, driven from Node with a stand-in WizardConnect manager that signs by inputPaths: Step Transaction Wallet request Gather coins from receive/1 at the owner address (receive/0) (sent by ensureCoinsAtOwner) 2 inputs at receive/1 Create plan (3 heirs, 30,000 sats for heirs + 2,000 fee budget) 7b9ef747c27c4f625e86742355eceb3ad8b278a85bcc0140913934622f4b1104 1 input at receive/0 I'm still here 41a8dca9e1d8ebc51a54555cfaeb153e20a989a27ddd7d9d8213ab2658e54b3f 3 inputs, wallet signs 1 Send to heirs (7,377 / 9,836 / 12,786) 703506e9e43f47ba80c481fd6e6452f3e67e5454f06f334cb9304f2eb7eddb5f 15 inputs, wallet signs 11 Reading state needs a connected contract: new StatefulContract(contract, category).state.deadline() on an unconnected instance fails with "Expected 1 data NFT(s) ... found 0"; .connect(provider) works. A timestamp locktime is final only below the median time past, and the contract needs locktime >= deadline, so a payout works only once the network clock is strictly past the deadline. Our first try at clock == deadline failed in preflight after the wallet had already signed a coin split. Design gap in our contract: the payout's network fee is paid by the presser's own coins, so the plan's feeBudget is never spent; it stays locked in the plan with the rounding dust (2,001 sats here). Either pay the fee from the fee budget or drop it. Tried and dropped (16 Nov): paying the reserve back to the caller. A contract cannot pay its own network fee (the SDK always funds the fee from the caller's coins), so the idea was to send what is left after the heirs back to tx.origin. Every form failed in the mock under real limits: this.transfer(tx.origin, this.balance) or (start - paid) after the ten heir slots stops in preflight with OP_VERIFY (the same with the owner's lock instead of tx.origin, so it is the draining transfer, not tx.origin); this.transfer(tx.origin, feeBudget) leaves the rounding dust and is refused with "Satoshi container remaining balance (2) is below dust threshold (576). Either transfer all satoshis (fully drain) or leave at least the dust minimum". Returning a value from the internal payHeir also pushed the 10-heir payout over the BCH-2026 operation-cost budget. So the reserve is what keeps the container above dust after a payout; the app now keeps 1,000 satoshis instead of 15,000 and says it stays in the plan.
